explain.say: In eleven years one young king marched from Greece to the edge of India, beat the Persian Empire and founded cities named after himself. He was dead at 32. Alexander of Macedon is still argued about over 2,300 years later. Look at the timeline of his short, violent life.

explain.say: Follow the map. From 334 BCE he crossed into Anatolia, won at Issus, went south to Egypt, where he founded Alexandria, then defeated Darius III at Gaugamela in 331. He took Babylon and Persepolis, crossed Afghanistan and reached the Punjab. That is many thousands of kilometres, mostly on foot. What kept the soldiers going?

items2: Greece > Turkey > Alexandria > Babylon > Persepolis > Afghanistan > Pakistan > Babylon
draw.label: Alexander's march, 334 to 323 BCE

explain.say: Look at 326 BCE. Beside the Beas River in the Punjab his exhausted army refused to march further east. He turned back, and in 323 BCE he died in Babylon. His generals, called the Diadochi, meaning successors, fought for decades and split the empire into kingdoms. Why might an empire built by one man fall apart so fast?

explain.say: Those kingdoms made the Hellenistic world, from Hellenes, the Greeks. The Ptolemies ruled Egypt from Alexandria with its great library, the Seleucids ruled from Syria to Iran, and Greek became a shared language from Egypt to Afghanistan, where archaeologists found a Greek city at Ai-Khanoum. Why would a shared language help trade and ideas?

explain.say: Was he a hero? See the debate. W. W. Tarn imagined a dreamer of human unity; A. B. Bosworth stressed massacres and terror, and later Persian texts called him the accursed. Brilliant work. Exam tip: our main source, Arrian, wrote about 450 years after Alexander, so say so.

faq.q: How far did Alexander the Great conquer?
faq.a: From Greece and Egypt across the Persian Empire to Central Asia and the Punjab in today's Pakistan and north-west India, between 334 and 325 BCE. His army refused to go further east at the Beas River in 326 BCE.

He died in Babylon in 323 BCE without a grown heir. His generals, the Diadochi, fought for about forty years and divided the empire into kingdoms, chiefly the Ptolemies in Egypt, the Seleucids in Asia and the Antigonids in Macedon.

It describes the period from Alexander's death in 323 BCE to Rome's conquest of Ptolemaic Egypt in 30 BCE, when Greek language and culture spread across the eastern Mediterranean and western Asia. The German historian Droysen popularised the term in the 1830s.
Founded by Alexander in Egypt in 331 BCE, Alexandria became the Ptolemies' capital and a great centre of learning, with its Library and Museum, where scholars like Euclid and Eratosthenes worked.
asks: What was the Library of Alexandria?

faq.q: Was Alexander a hero or a brutal conqueror?
faq.a: Historians disagree. Some, like W. W. Tarn, saw a visionary uniting peoples; others, like A. B. Bosworth, emphasise his massacres and ruthless rule. The surviving sources were written centuries later, which complicates both views.
asks: Was Alexander the Great really great?

facts: Alexander the Great died in Babylon in 323 BCE, aged 32.
Alexandria in Egypt was founded in 331 BCE.
The Hellenistic period is usually dated from 323 BCE to 30 BCE.
